# Introduction

Do web developers and machine learning (ML) developers occupy different positions or have different connection patterns in the GitHub social network? We investigate five questions:

1. Do the groups differ in their numbers of connections?
2. Do they differ in clustering and centrality?
3. Do developers of the same type connect more often than expected by chance?
4. Can network characteristics predict developer type?
5. Does network information improve prediction beyond profile attributes?

This is an exploratory analysis of one observed network. Group comparisons describe associations; they do not establish why developers form connections.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(igraph)
library(jsonlite)
library(Matrix)
library(glmnet)
library(pROC)
library(PRROC)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 120)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
type_colors <- c("Web" = "#2878A5", "ML" = "#D87528")
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
fmt_p <- function(x) format.pval(x, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
```

# Data and network construction

The [Stanford SNAP GitHub Social Network dataset](https://snap.stanford.edu/data/github-social.html) was collected in June 2019. Nodes represent developers who starred at least ten repositories; undirected edges represent mutual follower relationships. Developer type is derived from job titles. We interpret `ml_target = 0` as web and `ml_target = 1` as ML, following the original analysis.

Profile features are supplied as anonymized indices rather than named variables. We therefore use them as binary indicators and do not interpret particular coefficients as employer or location effects.

The following chunk downloads the original ZIP to temporary R-session storage. No separate data or results folders are needed. Node IDs are used explicitly to align labels, network measures, and profile features.

```{r}
#| label: load-data
temp_dir <- tempdir()
data_dir <- file.path(temp_dir, "git_web_ml")
required_files <- file.path(data_dir, c(
  "musae_git_edges.csv", "musae_git_target.csv", "musae_git_features.json"
))
if (!all(file.exists(required_files))) {
  temp_zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
  download.file("https://snap.stanford.edu/data/git_web_ml.zip",
                temp_zip, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  unzip(temp_zip, exdir = temp_dir)
  unlink(temp_zip)
}
edges <- read.csv(required_files[1])
nodes <- read.csv(required_files[2])
stopifnot(!anyNA(nodes$id), !anyDuplicated(nodes$id),
          !anyNA(nodes$ml_target), all(nodes$ml_target %in% c(0, 1)))

g <- graph_from_data_frame(edges[, 1:2], directed = FALSE,
                           vertices = data.frame(name = as.character(nodes$id)))
stopifnot(is_simple(g))
node_order <- match(V(g)$name, as.character(nodes$id))
stopifnot(!anyNA(node_order))
nodes <- nodes[node_order, ]
developer_type <- nodes$ml_target + 1L
n_nodes <- vcount(g)
n_edges <- ecount(g)

network_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Developers", "Mutual follower relationships", "Web developers",
              "ML developers", "Density", "Global transitivity"),
  Value = c(format(n_nodes, big.mark = ","), format(n_edges, big.mark = ","),
            sum(nodes$ml_target == 0), sum(nodes$ml_target == 1),
            fmt(edge_density(g), 6), fmt(transitivity(g), 4))
)
knitr::kable(network_summary, caption = "Characteristics of the observed network.")
```

The two groups are unequal in size: `r fmt(100 * mean(nodes$ml_target == 0), 1)`% of developers are web developers. This imbalance matters both for expected within-group connections and for classification evaluation.

# Question 1: Number of connections

A developer's degree is the number of other developers to whom they are connected. We summarize degree separately by developer type and use a logarithmic scale in the plot to display the long upper tail.

```{r}
#| label: degree-summary
eda_df <- data.frame(
  id = nodes$id,
  ml_target = nodes$ml_target,
  developer = factor(nodes$ml_target, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Web", "ML")),
  degree = as.numeric(degree(g))
)
degree_summary <- eda_df |>
  group_by(developer) |>
  summarise(N = n(), Mean = mean(degree), SD = sd(degree),
            Median = median(degree), IQR = IQR(degree), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(degree_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = "Degree distribution by developer type.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-degree
#| fig-cap: "Degree by developer type. The vertical axis uses log10(degree + 1)."
ggplot(eda_df, aes(developer, log10(degree + 1), fill = developer)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = type_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Developer type", y = "log10(degree + 1)")
```

We report the Wilcoxon rank-sum test as an exploratory comparison of degree distributions and Welch's test as a comparison of mean log-transformed degree. The Wilcoxon test is not generally a test of medians alone; the log transformation does not guarantee normality. Both procedures assume independent observations, an assumption that may fail for connected developers. Their conventional p-values therefore require caution.

```{r}
#| label: degree-tests
degree_wilcox <- wilcox.test(degree ~ developer, data = eda_df, exact = FALSE)
degree_welch <- t.test(log1p(degree) ~ developer, data = eda_df)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Test = c("Wilcoxon: degree", "Welch: log(1 + degree)"),
  Statistic = c(unname(degree_wilcox$statistic), unname(degree_welch$statistic)),
  `Conventional p-value` = c(fmt_p(degree_wilcox$p.value), fmt_p(degree_welch$p.value)),
  check.names = FALSE
), digits = 3)
```

Mean degree is `r fmt(mean(eda_df$degree[eda_df$developer == "Web"]))` for web developers and `r fmt(mean(eda_df$degree[eda_df$developer == "ML"]))` for ML developers. The descriptive difference is more directly interpretable here than a claim based solely on conventional significance tests.

# Question 2: Clustering and centrality

We measure local clustering (the fraction of possible neighbor-to-neighbor connections present), PageRank, betweenness, and eigenvector centrality. These measures capture different aspects of local cohesion and network position. Local clustering is assigned zero for nodes with fewer than two neighbors. Exact betweenness is calculated on the full graph and may make rendering take several minutes.

```{r}
#| label: centrality
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr digest::digest(list(g, eda_df))
eda_df$clustering <- transitivity(g, type = "local", isolates = "zero")
eda_df$pagerank <- page_rank(g)$vector
eda_df$betweenness <- betweenness(g, directed = FALSE, normalized = TRUE)
eda_df$eigenvector <- eigen_centrality(g)$vector
centrality_summary <- eda_df |>
  group_by(developer) |>
  summarise(across(c(clustering, pagerank, betweenness, eigenvector), median),
            .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(centrality_summary, digits = 6,
             caption = "Median clustering and centrality by developer type.")

metrics <- c("clustering", "pagerank", "betweenness", "eigenvector")
centrality_p <- vapply(metrics, function(metric) {
  wilcox.test(eda_df[[metric]] ~ eda_df$developer, exact = FALSE)$p.value
}, numeric(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = metrics,
  `Conventional p-value` = vapply(centrality_p, fmt_p, character(1)),
  `Holm-adjusted p-value` = vapply(p.adjust(centrality_p, "holm"), fmt_p, character(1)),
  check.names = FALSE
), caption = "Exploratory Wilcoxon comparisons; network dependence remains unaccounted for.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-clustering
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of local clustering by developer type."
ggplot(eda_df, aes(developer, clustering, fill = developer)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = type_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Developer type", y = "Local clustering coefficient")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pagerank
#| fig-cap: "PageRank by developer type on a logarithmic scale."
ggplot(eda_df, aes(developer, pagerank, fill = developer)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.15) + scale_y_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = type_colors, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Developer type", y = "PageRank (log scale)")
```

Holm adjustment addresses the four comparisons within this section, but does not correct network dependence. We treat these results as exploratory evidence about the observed graph.

# Question 3: Developer-type homophily

## Observed mixing

A high fraction of same-type edges is insufficient by itself to establish homophily: even random labeling produces many web-web edges when web developers form the majority. We first count each undirected edge once and compare the counts with their exact expectations when labels are assigned at random while group sizes remain fixed.

For group sizes $n_W$ and $n_M$ in a network with $n$ developers, the expected same-type edge fraction under this random-label null is

$$
P_{\mathrm{same}} =
\frac{n_W(n_W-1) + n_M(n_M-1)}{n(n-1)}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: mixing
edge_endpoints <- as_edgelist(g, names = FALSE)
type_from <- developer_type[edge_endpoints[, 1]]
type_to <- developer_type[edge_endpoints[, 2]]
edge_category <- ifelse(type_from == 1 & type_to == 1, "Web-Web",
                        ifelse(type_from == 2 & type_to == 2, "ML-ML", "Web-ML"))
mixing_summary <- data.frame(connection = factor(
  edge_category, levels = c("Web-Web", "Web-ML", "ML-ML")
)) |> count(connection, .drop = FALSE)
group_sizes <- tabulate(developer_type, nbins = 2)
expected_fraction <- c(
  group_sizes[1] * (group_sizes[1] - 1),
  2 * prod(group_sizes),
  group_sizes[2] * (group_sizes[2] - 1)
) / (n_nodes * (n_nodes - 1))
mixing_summary$observed_percent <- 100 * mixing_summary$n / n_edges
mixing_summary$expected_edges <- n_edges * expected_fraction
mixing_summary$expected_percent <- 100 * expected_fraction
same_type_fraction <- mean(type_from == type_to)
expected_same <- sum(expected_fraction[c(1, 3)])
knitr::kable(mixing_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = "Observed mixing and expectations under random labeling.")
```

Same-type edges account for **`r fmt(100 * same_type_fraction)`%** of connections, compared with **`r fmt(100 * expected_same)`%** under random labeling: a difference of **`r fmt(100 * (same_type_fraction - expected_same))` percentage points**. This excess is concentrated in Web-Web connections, with `r format(mixing_summary$n[1], big.mark = ",")` observed versus approximately `r format(round(mixing_summary$expected_edges[1]), big.mark = ",")` expected. ML-ML connections are only slightly above their random-label expectation, with `r format(mixing_summary$n[3], big.mark = ",")` observed versus approximately `r format(round(mixing_summary$expected_edges[3]), big.mark = ",")` expected. These comparisons account for unequal group sizes, but random labeling does not preserve differences in connectivity between the groups.

## Assortativity

We quantify categorical mixing using [Newman's nominal assortativity coefficient as implemented in igraph](https://r.igraph.org/reference/assortativity.html):

$$
r = \frac{\sum_i e_{ii} - \sum_i a_i^2}{1-\sum_i a_i^2},
\qquad a_i = \sum_j e_{ij}.
$$

For an undirected graph, $e_{ij}$ is the fraction of oriented edge connections from group $i$ to group $j$, with each undirected edge contributing in both directions. The marginal $a_i$ is therefore the fraction of all edge endpoints belonging to group $i$. Unlike the random-label expectation above, which depends on the numbers of developers in each group, assortativity uses the groups' shares of edge endpoints. This distinction matters because groups with higher average degree contribute disproportionately many endpoints.

In this network, web developers account for approximately `r fmt(100 * (2 * mixing_summary$n[1] + mixing_summary$n[2]) / (2 * n_edges))`% of edge endpoints and ML developers account for `r fmt(100 * (2 * mixing_summary$n[3] + mixing_summary$n[2]) / (2 * n_edges))`%. The assortativity baseline for same-type mixing is therefore $a_W^2+a_M^2$, or approximately `r fmt(100 * sum(((2 * mixing_summary$n[c(1, 3)] + mixing_summary$n[2]) / (2 * n_edges))^2))`%, compared with the observed `r fmt(100 * same_type_fraction)`%. The coefficient divides this excess by the maximum possible excess above that baseline. Positive assortativity indicates more same-type mixing than the endpoint-based baseline, zero indicates agreement with that baseline, and negative assortativity indicates less same-type mixing.

```{r}
#| label: assortativity
observed_assortativity <- assortativity_nominal(
  g, types = developer_type, directed = FALSE
)
```

Observed assortativity is **`r fmt(observed_assortativity, 4)`**.

## Random-label permutation test

The null hypothesis is that developer labels are exchangeable across vertices, conditional on the observed network and group sizes. The one-sided alternative is that assortativity is greater than under this null.

We hold the entire graph fixed and shuffle developer labels $B=999$ times. The test statistic is **assortativity**, consistent with the assortativity analysis above. The Monte Carlo p-value is

$$
\widehat p = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^{B} I(r_b \geq r_{\mathrm{obs}})}{B+1}.
$$

This uses the network as a whole rather than treating its edges as independent observations.

```{r}
#| label: permutation-test
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr digest::digest(list(g, developer_type, observed_assortativity))
set.seed(636)
B <- 999L
permuted_assortativity <- replicate(B, {
  assortativity_nominal(g, types = sample(developer_type), directed = FALSE)
})
n_exceed <- sum(permuted_assortativity >= observed_assortativity)
permutation_p <- (1 + n_exceed) / (B + 1)
homophily_results <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Observed assortativity", "Mean permuted assortativity",
              "Permutations at least as large as observed", "Permutations",
              "One-sided Monte Carlo p-value"),
  Value = c(fmt(observed_assortativity, 4), fmt(mean(permuted_assortativity), 4),
            n_exceed, B, fmt(permutation_p, 4))
)
knitr::kable(homophily_results, caption = "Random-label permutation test of assortativity.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-permutation
#| fig-cap: "Assortativity after randomly shuffling developer labels. The red line marks the observed value."
ggplot(data.frame(assortativity = permuted_assortativity), aes(assortativity)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#2878A5", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_assortativity, color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Categorical assortativity", y = "Number of permutations")
```

The observed value was met or exceeded by **`r n_exceed` of `r B`** permutations, giving **$\widehat p =$ `r fmt(permutation_p, 4)`**. `r if (observed_assortativity > 0 && permutation_p < 0.05) "This provides evidence of positive same-type mixing relative to the random-label null." else "This does not establish positive same-type mixing beyond the random-label null at the 5% level."` With 999 permutations, the smallest possible reported p-value is 0.001; zero exceedances do not imply a true p-value of zero.

## Interpretation and limitations

The observed network shows positive developer-type assortativity, and **`r n_exceed` of `r B`** random label assignments produced an assortativity coefficient at least as large as the observed value. This supports an association between developer type and the pattern of connections. It does not establish that specialization causes developers to choose same-type connections; employer, location, and existing communities may also contribute.

The mixing table and assortativity coefficient use different baselines and therefore provide complementary descriptions. Although ML-ML connections are close to their expectation under random labeling, this does not imply an absence of assortative mixing involving ML developers. Random labeling uses group sizes, whereas assortativity uses edge-endpoint shares. The latter baseline reflects the fact that ML developers contribute a smaller share of connection endpoints than their share of vertices.

The permutation test asks whether the observed assortativity is unusually large when developer labels are exchangeable across vertices of the fixed graph. Each shuffle preserves the graph and group sizes, but changes which vertices carry each label and therefore changes the groups' degree distributions and endpoint shares. Thus, this test does not establish assortative mixing beyond what might be associated with differences in degree. Shuffling labels within degree strata would provide a useful sensitivity analysis by approximately preserving the relationship between developer type and degree.

# Question 4: Predicting developer type from network characteristics

A goal of ours is to determine whether we can predict whether someone is a web or machine learning developer. To do so, we constructed a dataset where each node is an observation and each predictor is derived from network characteristics such as degree, PageRank, clustering coefficient, betweenness centrality, eigenvector centrality, and spectral embedding coordinates derived from singular value decomposition. We then fit a classification model (regularized logistic regression (Lasso)) to predict whether the node is a web or ML developer.

## Scree plot

To decide on the right number of dimensions, or the number of coordinate columns we want our singular value decomposition (and ultimately our adjacency spectral embedding) to output, we look at a scree plot which ranks dimensions by how much structural weight or importance they carry. For the symmetric adjacency matrix, the magnitudes of its eigenvalues are its singular values. We inspect the 40 largest magnitudes and mark candidate dimensions 3, 5, and 10.

The scree plot indicates an elbow at $d=5$ (the green line), providing a choice that captures important network structure without making the model too complex. We use five dimensions for the adjacency spectral embedding. We also compute an automated profile-likelihood dimension selection as a diagnostic.

```{r}
#| label: spectral-features
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr digest::digest(g)
set.seed(42)
adjacency_spectrum <- spectrum(
  g, algorithm = "arpack", which = list(pos = "lm", howmany = 40)
)
top_evals <- sort(abs(adjacency_spectrum$values), decreasing = TRUE)
optimal_d <- dim_select(top_evals)
d_chosen <- 5L

# Reuse igraph's sparse spectral implementation; no dense adjacency matrix.
# cvec = 0 specifies the original, unaugmented adjacency matrix.
set.seed(42)
ase_result <- embed_adjacency_matrix(
  g, no = d_chosen, weights = NA, which = "lm", scaled = TRUE,
  cvec = rep(0, vcount(g))
)
ase_matrix <- ase_result$X
colnames(ase_matrix) <- paste0("ASE_Dim", seq_len(d_chosen))
stopifnot(nrow(ase_matrix) == nrow(eda_df), all(is.finite(ase_matrix)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-spectral-scree
#| fig-cap: "The 40 largest absolute adjacency eigenvalues, with candidate embedding dimensions."
plot(top_evals, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#2878A5",
     xlab = "Eigenvalue index", ylab = "Absolute eigenvalue",
     main = "GitHub adjacency spectrum")
abline(v = c(3, 5, 10), col = c("firebrick", "forestgreen", "blue"), lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("d = 3", "d = 5 (selected)", "d = 10"),
       col = c("firebrick", "forestgreen", "blue"), lty = 2, bty = "n")
```

The profile-likelihood diagnostic selects **`r optimal_d`** dimensions; the fitted models use **`r d_chosen`**. For an undirected graph, ASE scales the selected eigenvectors by the square roots of the absolute eigenvalues. Coordinates remain aligned with the node IDs used throughout the report.

## Lasso model and shared comparison design

Question 4 evaluates the network-only model. To support Question 5, we fit three lasso logistic regression models using the same training and test developers:

| Model | Predictors |
| --- | --- |
| Profile only | Supplied binary profile features |
| Network only | Degree, clustering, PageRank, betweenness, eigenvector centrality, five ASE coordinates |
| Combined | Both sets of predictors |

For a predictor vector $x_i$, each model takes the form

$$
\log\left\{\frac{P(Y_i=1\mid x_i)}{1-P(Y_i=1\mid x_i)}\right\}
= \beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta,
$$

with an $L_1$ penalty on coefficients. Here $Y_i=1$ denotes an ML developer. The lasso penalty can set redundant or weak predictor coefficients to zero.

## Feature alignment and evaluation design

The JSON is keyed by node ID. We explicitly reorder its entries to match the network before creating the sparse binary feature matrix. We use a stratified 70/30 split and five stratified cross-validation folds within the training set. All models share those folds. The penalty is chosen by training cross-validation ROC-AUC; test ROC-AUC is reported only after fitting.

`glmnet` standardizes predictors within each fit, avoiding full-dataset scaling before the split. Network measures and ASE are computed on the full observed graph without using developer labels. Consequently, this is a **transductive** experiment: it predicts unknown labels for developers whose connections are already known. Random node splitting does not test transfer to independent communities or future developers.

```{r}
#| label: classification-data
node_features <- fromJSON(required_files[3], simplifyVector = FALSE)
feature_order <- match(as.character(eda_df$id), names(node_features))
stopifnot(!anyNA(feature_order))
node_features <- lapply(node_features[feature_order], as.integer)
feature_ids <- unlist(node_features, use.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyNA(feature_ids), all(feature_ids >= 0))
feature_matrix <- sparseMatrix(
  i = rep(seq_along(node_features), lengths(node_features)),
  j = feature_ids + 1L, x = 1,
  dims = c(nrow(eda_df), max(feature_ids) + 1L)
)
network_matrix <- cbind(as.matrix(eda_df[, c(
  "degree", "pagerank", "clustering", "betweenness", "eigenvector"
)]), ase_matrix)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(network_matrix)))
combined_matrix <- cbind(feature_matrix, Matrix(network_matrix, sparse = TRUE))
y <- eda_df$ml_target

set.seed(42)
train_index <- sort(unlist(lapply(split(seq_along(y), y), function(index) {
  sample(index, floor(0.7 * length(index)))
}), use.names = FALSE))
test_index <- setdiff(seq_along(y), train_index)
y_train <- y[train_index]
y_test <- y[test_index]
fold_id <- integer(length(train_index))
for (label in c(0, 1)) {
  index <- which(y_train == label)
  fold_id[index] <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(index)))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fit-models
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr digest::digest(list(feature_matrix, network_matrix, combined_matrix, train_index, test_index, y_train, y_test, fold_id))
predictor_sets <- list("Profile only" = feature_matrix,
                       "Network only" = network_matrix,
                       "Combined" = combined_matrix)
fits <- lapply(predictor_sets, function(x) {
  cv.glmnet(x[train_index, , drop = FALSE], y_train,
            family = "binomial", alpha = 1, standardize = TRUE,
            foldid = fold_id, type.measure = "auc")
})
test_probabilities <- lapply(names(predictor_sets), function(model) {
  as.numeric(predict(fits[[model]],
    newx = predictor_sets[[model]][test_index, , drop = FALSE],
    s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))
})
names(test_probabilities) <- names(predictor_sets)
roc_objects <- lapply(test_probabilities, function(probability) {
  roc(y_test, probability, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)
})
test_auc <- vapply(roc_objects, function(object) as.numeric(auc(object)), numeric(1))
model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = names(test_auc),
  `Test ROC-AUC` = unname(test_auc),
  `Selected lambda` = vapply(fits, function(fit) fit$lambda.min, numeric(1)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(model_comparison, digits = 4,
             caption = "Held-out performance on the same test developers.")
```

## Results from Lasso

```{r}
#| label: q4-coefficients
q4_coefficients <- as.matrix(coef(fits[["Network only"]], s = "lambda.min"))
# glmnet returns coefficients on the original predictor scales.
# Multiply by training SDs to express slopes per training standard deviation.
q4_training_sd <- apply(network_matrix[train_index, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
q4_standardized <- q4_coefficients[, 1]
q4_standardized[-1] <- q4_standardized[-1] * q4_training_sd
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Predictor = rownames(q4_coefficients),
  Coefficient = q4_coefficients[, 1],
  `Coefficient per training SD` = q4_standardized,
  check.names = FALSE
), digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
caption = "Network-only lasso coefficients; zero indicates a predictor excluded by the penalty.")
```

Since we are predicting ML developer (ML = 1, Web = 0), a positive coefficient means that the feature predicts an ML developer while a negative coefficient indicates that the feature predicts a web developer, holding the other predictors fixed. The coefficient table shows both the original predictor scale and the effect per training standard deviation so that features on different scales can be compared.

PageRank describes the importance of a developer's connections within the network, while degree describes how many connections a developer has. A positive PageRank coefficient and negative degree coefficient would indicate that, despite having fewer connections, ML developers' connections may be with influential individuals within the network. Eigenvector centrality similarly reflects connections to central developers, while betweenness describes a developer's role as a bridge between different subcommunities. These coefficient interpretations describe associations within the model.

The five-dimensional coordinates from the adjacency spectral embedding allow the model to capture latent connectivity patterns beyond the centrality metrics. A dimension with a zero coefficient is dropped by the lasso model; dimensions that remain in the model contribute to predicting ML and web developers. The signs of the ASE coordinates are arbitrary, so interpretation focuses on the connectivity information they add rather than the direction of an individual coordinate.

```{r}
#| label: q4-performance
q4_probability <- test_probabilities[["Network only"]]
pr_q4 <- PRROC::pr.curve(
  scores.class0 = q4_probability[y_test == 1],
  scores.class1 = q4_probability[y_test == 0],
  curve = TRUE
)
q4_pr_baseline <- mean(y_test == 1)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = c("Test ROC-AUC", "Test PR-AUC", "Test ML prevalence (PR baseline)"),
  Value = c(test_auc["Network only"], pr_q4$auc.integral, q4_pr_baseline)
), digits = 4, caption = "Held-out network-only performance, treating ML as the positive class.")
```

## ROC curve

```{r}
#| label: fig-q4-roc
#| fig-cap: "Held-out ROC curve for the network-only model."
plot(roc_objects[["Network only"]], col = "#D87528", lwd = 2,
     legacy.axes = TRUE, main = "Question 4: Network-only ROC curve")
```

The ROC curve shows how well network structure predicts developer type, with an AUC of **`r fmt(test_auc["Network only"], 3)`**.

## Precision-recall AUC

Because web developers outnumber machine learning developers roughly 3-to-1, we also evaluated the Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC).

```{r}
#| label: fig-q4-pr
#| fig-cap: "Held-out precision-recall curve for ML developers; the dashed line marks test-set ML prevalence."
plot(pr_q4, color = "#2878A5", main = "Question 4: Precision-recall curve")
abline(h = q4_pr_baseline, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
```

The model achieved a PR-AUC of **`r fmt(pr_q4$auc.integral, 3)`**, compared with the random-ranking baseline of **`r fmt(q4_pr_baseline, 3)`**, the proportion of ML developers in the test set. Performance above this baseline indicates that the network features help identify the minority machine learning class despite the skewed dataset.

# Question 5: Does network information improve prediction beyond profile attributes?

The profile-only, network-only, and combined models above use identical held-out developers and training folds. The network and combined models both include the five ASE coordinates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-roc
#| fig-cap: "Test-set ROC curves for the three predictor sets."
roc_colors <- c("#2878A5", "#D87528", "#31844A")
plot(roc_objects[[1]], col = roc_colors[1], lwd = 2, legacy.axes = TRUE,
     main = "Predicting ML developer labels")
for (i in 2:3) lines(roc_objects[[i]], col = roc_colors[i], lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", sprintf("%s (AUC %.3f)", names(test_auc), test_auc),
       col = roc_colors, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The network-only model achieves a test ROC-AUC of **`r fmt(test_auc["Network only"], 3)`**. The combined model has ROC-AUC **`r fmt(test_auc["Combined"], 3)`**, compared with **`r fmt(test_auc["Profile only"], 3)`** for profile attributes alone. The combined-minus-profile difference is **`r fmt(test_auc["Combined"] - test_auc["Profile only"], 4)`**.

This single split estimates predictive performance for the stated setting. A small AUC difference alone does not establish a reliable improvement. Repeated splits or community-based validation would help assess stability and generalization. The Question 4 PR curve supplements ROC-AUC for the minority ML class; threshold-specific measures would further describe the practical tradeoff between false positives and missed ML developers.

# Discussion and next steps

The report separates descriptive group differences, random-label evidence about homophily, and predictive comparisons. These answer related but distinct questions. Conventional node-level tests and random train/test splits require particular care because developers are connected.

The next analysis priorities are to assess homophily conditional on degree, evaluate model stability with splits that reflect the intended prediction setting, and examine minority-class performance. Conclusions concern the observed 2019 network rather than all GitHub users or current developer behavior.
